title: paper-garden-curation-and-conference-scrapbook
body:
Quick note: this is a lightweight personal scratchbook from the workshop and a handful of papers I skimmed in the last two weeks. Not polished — half ideas, half todo list. Meant to be a place to stash takeaways and experiment sketches before I either make a proper PR or throw it away.

Top-level takeaways (TL;DR)
- Mixture of small kernel improvements + smarter KV/cache heuristics looks like the fastest path to cut tail latency on long-context workloads.
- Eval design matters: a few long-tail prompt templates can blow up apparent regression rates when you change quantization or batch size.
- Conference talk highlight: simple instrumentation (per-token timing + first-byte variance) surfaces pathological requests way earlier than avg-latency dashboards.

Papers / blog clippings I want to remember (short bullet summaries)
- "Efficient KV Cache Compression" (notes on arXiv paper): good analysis of block-level compression vs token-level; major win when repetition across windows is high. Tradeoffs: compression latency vs GPU memory bandwidth. For our serving runtime — could be selective: only compress >N tokens or when free-memory threshold hits.
- "Latency-aware batching strategies" (workshop slides): adaptive batching that drops into a low-latency mode for requests flagged as interactive. Flagging heuristics can be lightweight (header + recent-pings) rather than content-based.
- "Quantization and calibration drift" (deep-dive blog): small quant changes introduce distributional shifts in logits that propagate to downstream evals; recommend adding a tiny calibration step (2-3 tokens) on rollout candidate models.

Conference/workshop takeaways (redacted notes)
- Speaker: A. Sorensen — 'Measure before optimize' — anecdote: their team had a 30% cost regression after enabling more batching because they missed a skew in prefix lengths. Action: add token-length histograms to per-route dashboards.
- Panel: 'Serving under constraints' — consensus: routing by SLO (latency) first, cost second. Model fallbacks should be priority-ordered with compatibility metadata (max-seqlen, kv-encoding, quant-profile).
- Ops tip: preserve first-byte timing per route and emit a 95/99/100ms bucket flag for spike detection.

Experiment sketches (quick, runnable)
1) Selective KV compression pilot
- Hypothesis: compressing KV blocks only for requests > 2048 tokens yields >20% memory headroom with <5% latency inflation for p50.
- Experiment: add flag compress_kv_if_length_above=2048 in runtime canary; compare p50/p95/p99 and memory usage.
- Metrics: tokens/sec, mem headroom (GB), p50/p95/p99 latency, error rate.
- Risk: CPU/GPU bandwidth trade; fallback is to revert compression or raise threshold.

2) Tiny calibration on model rollout
- Hypothesis: adding a 3-token calibration (softmax-temperature adjust) reduces eval regression rate on QA suites after quantization.
- Implementation: inject 3 warmup tokens, compute temperature multiplier on logits, then proceed.
- Measure: BLEU/EM-type metrics for small eval suite + human-read QA sample.

3) Interactive request fast-path based on header flag
- Idea: allow the client to mark requests as interactive; runtime prioritizes those, reduces batch window to 5ms.
- Sanity checks: ensure quota/rate limiting still applies; track abuse patterns.

Unresolved questions / open curiosities
- How often do real workloads contain long repeating spans where compression is beneficial? (Need trace sampling)
- Does small calibration bias outputs in corner cases (hallucination increase?) — need careful human spot checks.
- If we compress KV, what format is safest across fallback models (different vocab/tokenization)? Must keep format model-agnostic or provide conversion layers.

Action items (me / short horizon)
- [ ] Add a lightweight trace-sampler job that emits token-length histograms (route, model, prefix_len, session_id hashed) — low sample rate (0.1%) and store 30 days. Target: prototype by 2026-11-12.
- [ ] Spin up selective-KV-compression canary on a dev cluster; reuse PR in linked_artifacts PR #42 as baseline.
- [ ] Draft a one-pager for the eval-calibration idea and run it by Maya before proposing as canary.

Notes to self (scrappy / half-formed)
- If we add header-driven interactive flag, also add a token-charge multiplier to discourage abuse (cost more $ for low-latency path) — simplest immediate lever.
- Consider a multi-tiered compression: cheap lightweight LZ for short deltas, and heavier block compression for >10k tokens.
- Quick local test: take a 50k token session trace, try gzip vs lz4 on 512-token blocks and measure decode latency on CPU thread pool.

Useful links I scribbled down
- arXiv efficient-kv: https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.04332 (compression/kv ideas)
- Workshop slides (internal): CONFLUENCE-REDWOOD-1234
- KV pilot PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/kv-cache-experiments/pull/42

Random scatterbrain (for future discussion)
- What if we defined 'semantic checkpointing' — store compressed representations of earlier context and only expand on demand? Could help super-long sessions but needs semantic-to-token fidelity tests.
- Is there a way to trade a bit of coherence for massive memory savings for archival context? e.g., store topic vectors and regenerate short summaries on re-entry.

If I forget: next time I attend a talk, bring a 2-column notepad: left=measurement signal they added, right=potential cheap pilot we could run. That framing helps ship tiny experiments.

End of scratchpad. Will move top items into a proper proposal if any of the pilots show promise.
